summary.text: Proteins are large molecules made of one or more long chains of amino acid residues.
They do many jobs in living things, including speeding up reactions, copying DNA, giving cells structure and moving molecules around.
A protein's amino acid sequence, set by its gene, usually makes it fold into a specific 3D structure that determines its activity.

paragraphs.heading: What a protein is
paragraphs.text: A protein is a large molecule made of one or more long chains of amino acid residues. A single straight chain of residues is called a polypeptide, and every protein has at least one long one. The residues are linked to each other by peptide bonds. Short chains, under about 20 to 30 residues, are rarely counted as proteins and usually go by the name peptides.

paragraphs.heading: The jobs they do
paragraphs.text: Proteins do a huge range of work inside living things. They speed up metabolic reactions, copy DNA, respond to signals, give cells and bodies their structure, and carry molecules from place to place. Many are enzymes, which speed up the chemical reactions that metabolism depends on. Some have structural or mechanical roles, like actin and myosin in muscle, or the scaffolding proteins that keep a cell in shape. Others take part in cell signaling, immune responses, cells sticking together, and the cell cycle.

paragraphs.heading: From gene to shape
paragraphs.text: What mainly sets one protein apart from another is its order of amino acids, and that order is written in a gene. The order usually makes the protein fold into a particular 3D shape, and that shape decides what it does. The genetic code generally calls for 20 standard amino acids, though some organisms add selenocysteine and certain archaea add pyrrolysine. During or soon after a protein is made, its residues are often chemically changed, which can alter its folding, stability and function. Some proteins also need a helper that is not a protein, such as an ion, to work; these helpers are called cofactors.

paragraphs.heading: Made, used, recycled
paragraphs.text: Proteins do not last forever. After a while the cell breaks them down and reuses the parts, a cycle called protein turnover. How long one lasts is given as its half-life, which can run from minutes to years, with an average of 1 to 2 days in mammal cells. Faulty or misfolded proteins are cleared faster, often by the proteasome, which is itself a big assembly of proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Protein in the diet
paragraphs.text: Animals need protein in their food to get the essential amino acids their bodies cannot build. Digestion breaks dietary protein into amino acids that refill the body's free supply. Most of that supply goes into new body proteins, but it also matters for energy and for making other molecules that contain nitrogen. Thomas Burr Osborne and Lafayette Mendel pinned down several essential amino acids by feeding lab rats, and rats on a diet missing one of them grew poorly.

paragraphs.heading: Naming the molecule
paragraphs.text: People have studied proteins since the 1700s, when Antoine Fourcroy and others lumped them together as albumins. The Dutch chemist Gerardus Johannes Mulder described them, and the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius named them in 1838. The name comes from a Greek word meaning primary, or in the lead. Mulder wrongly guessed that all proteins might be one single kind of very large molecule.

paragraphs.heading: A gift from a hot dog maker
paragraphs.text: Early researchers struggled because proteins were hard to purify. Blood, egg whites and keratin gave plenty of protein in bulk, but not single proteins on their own. During the 1950s, the Armour Hot Dog Company made 1 kg of pure bovine pancreatic ribonuclease A and handed it out to scientists for free. That gift helped make ribonuclease A a major subject of study for decades.
